title: Leakage benchmarking with decohering subgroups in the presence of preparation and measurement errors
authors: Shawn Geller, Tongyu Zhao, Alex Kwiatkowski, Scott Glancy, Raymond W. Simmonds, Emanuel Knill
abstract: A common problem with physical qubits is that the state can leak outside the computational subspace. To characterize the problem, it is desirable to measure both the leakage probability and the fidelity of gates inside the computational subspace. Randomized benchmarking is a readily accessible method for estimating average gate fidelities and can be modified to account for leakage. However, in the presence of state preparation and measurement errors (SPAM) there are parameter degeneracies, and fidelities and leakage become underdetermined. We study the example of qudits with any number of leakage levels under the assumption of gate-independent noise. We show that randomized benchmarking sequences with leakage level decoherence can be analyzed as a Markov process with noisy classical preparations and measurements. This result generalizes to randomized benchmarking with random gates from an arbitrary group that contains a phase-decohering subgroup. We characterize the parameter degeneracy in inferring the Markov process, preparations and measurements. Based on this characterization we develop a measurement and inference method taking advantage of known conservative bounds on SPAM to constrain fidelity, leakage and other parameters of the Markov process, state preparations and measurements. As part of our study, we experimentally implemented the measurement method for a qubit defined on the one-excitation subspace of two transmons, for which there are two leakage levels. We determined confidence intervals accounting for parameter degeneracy for a number of performance parameters of the system. For leakage and fidelity, we compare these intervals to those obtained for several conventional methods for leakage benchmarking.
summary: This paper presents an advanced benchmarking technique, Decohering Subgroup Randomized Benchmarking (DSRB), to characterize quantum gate performance in the presence of leakage and state preparation/measurement errors. By modeling the system as a Markov process and incorporating physical constraints, the authors develop a robust inference method. This method allows for the determination of reliable confidence intervals for critical performance metrics like fidelity and leakage rate, which is crucial for scaling quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately characterizing qubit gate fidelity and leakage probability when the physical system suffers from State Preparation and Measurement (SPAM) errors.
main_result: The authors developed a measurement and inference method that uses known conservative bounds on SPAM to constrain the underdetermined parameters, yielding experimentally validated confidence intervals for fidelity and leakage.
method: They model the process using Decohering Subgroup Randomized Benchmarking (DSRB) and employ advanced inference techniques, including constrained optimization and checking parameter feasibility across multiple orthants.
model_or_system: The study focuses on physical qubits, exemplified by a qubit defined on the one-excitation subspace of two transmon qubits, which exhibits both a computational subspace and leakage levels.
key_observables: Average gate fidelities, total leakage rate, and the parameters defining the Markov process (e.g., transition probabilities).
important_parameters: Leakage probability, seepage probability, and the parameters defining the Markov process's transition matrix.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes gate-independent noise and relies on applying conservative, known bounds on SPAM errors to resolve parameter degeneracies.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the four levels of the two transmon qubits, defining the computational subspace and the leakage subspace, and detailing leakage and seepage probabilities per step.
paper_structure: The paper details the system model, develops the DSRB theory, outlines the maximum likelihood inference framework, applies the method to the dual-rail transmon qubit, and concludes with experimental results comparing DSRB against conventional benchmarking methods.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, theoretically grounded framework for benchmarking real quantum hardware, directly addressing the practical limitations imposed by noise sources like leakage and imperfect state preparation.
